oldContent: We Work Remotely: Remote jobs in design, programming, marketing and more https://weworkremotely.com/remote-jobs.rss We Work Remotely: Remote jobs in design, programming, marketing and more en-US 60 Veeva Systems: IT Consultant - Solutions Architect - Cloud CRM (Remote) Anywhere in the World Adobe Creative Suite, Community Growth, Competitor Analysis, Accounting, Architect, Architecture, Blog Writing, Editing, Audio Editing, and Brand Identity Design Customer Support Full-Time <img src="https://we-work-remotely.imgix.net/logos/0171/6697/logo.gif?ixlib=rails-4.0.0&w=50&h=50&dpr=2&fit=fill&auto=compress" /> <p> <strong>Headquarters:</strong> Hungary - Budapest <br /><strong>URL:</strong> <a href="http://veeva.com">http://veeva.com</a> </p> <div class="content"><div class="section-wrapper page-full-width"><div class="section page-centered"><div><span>Veeva Systems is a mission-driven organization and pioneer in industry cloud, helping life sciences companies bring therapies to patients faster. As one of the fastest-growing SaaS companies in history, we surpassed $3B in revenue in our last fiscal year with extensive growth potential ahead.</span></div> <div>&nbsp;</div> <div><span>At the heart of Veeva are our values: Do the Right Thing, Customer Success, Employee Success, and Speed. We're not just any public company – we made history in 2021 by becoming a&nbsp;</span><a href="https://medium.com/@peter.gassner/public-benefit-corporation-pbc-486e1e9508a6"><span>public benefit corporation</span></a><span>&nbsp;(PBC), legally bound to balancing the interests of customers, employees, society, and investors.</span></div> <div>&nbsp;</div> <div><span>As a&nbsp;</span><a href="https://careers.veeva.com/work-anywhere/"><span>Work Anywhere</span></a><span>&nbsp;company, we support your flexibility to work from home or in the office, so you can thrive in your ideal environment.</span></div> <div>&nbsp;</div> <div><span>Join us in&nbsp;</span><a href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TaPSP8cCSKY&amp;ab_channel=Forbes"><span>transforming the life sciences industry</span></a><span>, committed to making a positive impact on its customers, employees, and communities.</span></div><div><br></div><h3><span>The Role</span></h3> <div>Are you looking for a place where your work makes an impact? We are seeking a talented Cloud CRM Consultant to join our amazing, fast-paced team of experts in Hungary.</div> <div>&nbsp;</div> <div>The Senior Cloud CRM Consultant is a member of our Commercial Managed Services team who provides ongoing professional service for customers live with Veeva’s commercial solutions.</div> <div>&nbsp;</div> <div>You will provide application consulting and serve as the strategic bridge between business stakeholders and technical teams, ensuring systems are scalable, secure, and built to drive business value primarily on the Vault CRM application, but will potentially develop expertise across other Commercial products. The post Baidu Releases ERNIE 5.5 Flash Base: A 280B MoE Base Model With 14B Active Parameters appeared first on MarkTechPost . ]]> Baidu has released ERNIE 5.5 Flash Base , the raw pre-training checkpoint of its new sparse Mixture-of-Experts language model. ERNIE 5.5 Flash Base is a 280B-parameter text model from Baidu that activates 14B parameters per token. The weights stop at the end of pre-training, with no mid- or post-training applied. This as a clean starting point for teams that want to compare fine-tuning, instruction tuning or RL methods from one checkpoint. TL;DR Size: 280B total, 14B active per token; 128K training context, 1M for fine-tuning and inference. Runs on: Multi-GPU servers. Baidu’s reference configs use 4-way parallelism in SGLang and vLLM. GPU model and VRAM not disclosed. FP8 and BF16 weights. Performance: Best score on 24 of 30 base-model benchmarks in Baidu’s unified pipeline (self-reported). Best: MMLU-Pro 78.4, ahead of DeepSeek-V4-Flash-Base at 69.2. Worst: HELMET-Rerank 56.2, behind DeepSeek-V4-Flash-Base at 60.0. What is ERNIE 5.5 Flash Base? It is a text-only MoE base model with 43 layers and a 4096 hidden size . It was pre-trained from scratch on 33.5T tokens with the Muon optimizer. The tokenizer has 201,216 entries and groups numbers right-to-left in chunks of up to 3 digits. Activated compute, KV cache and long-context cost were treated as one budget. Pre-training data leaned on repository-scale code and long-context material, since those are hard to add later. How does the ERNIE 5.5 Flash architecture work? Hybrid attention : 37 layers use Heavily Compressed Attention (HCA), which caches 1 entry per 128 tokens. The other 6 layers use Multi-head Latent Attention with sparse attention (MLA + DSA). That means 1 in 7 layers keeps full-context access. HCA layers use 512-dim heads; MLA layers use 256-dim heads. Gated and mixed heads : The attention output gate comes from the low-rank query latent, cutting gate-projection parameters by 75%. Virtual Head Attention adds a lightweight low-rank mix across heads. Multi-Router Latent MoE. Each MoE layer has 512 routed experts (top-10) plus 1 shared expert. Several independent sigmoid routers replace a single router, per Baidu’s Multi-Router paper . Expert FLOPs and communication volume stay unchanged. Experts run in a 2048-d latent space, half the hidden width. ECHO instead of MTP. : ECHO reuses the backbone’s final layer to predict future tokens. The same layer doubles as a built-in draft model for speculative decoding. ECHO adds 0.36B parameters, excluded from the headline counts. Other pieces : The model uses Manifold-constrained Hyper-Connections with expansion rate 4 and a MultiMax output head. How does ERNIE 5.5 Flash Base perform on benchmarks? Baidu team evaluated all 4 models with the same pipeline, prompts and few-shot settings. All figures below are self-reported by Baidu. Exams: MMLU 93.3, MMLU-Redux 94.1, MMLU-Pro 78.4. Knowledge: SimpleQA 34.1, versus 29.1 for DeepSeek-V4-Flash-Base. STEM and reasoning: GPQA 60.2, MGSM 87.0, BBH direct 77.1. Code: HumanEval+ 82.3, MBPP+ 81.5, LiveCodeBench 40.1. Long context: RepoQA 91.7, LongBench-v2 48.7, HELMET-ICL 85.9. It loses on 6 tasks. DeepSeek-V4-Flash-Base leads on ChineseSimpleQA, INCLUDE-lite, HELMET-Rerank and InfiniteBench. Hy3-preview-Base leads on BBH CoT and FullStackBench. Competitor numbers in Baidu’s pipeline differ slightly from each vendor’s own report. DeepSeek lists MMLU-Pro 68.3; Baidu measures 69.2. Tencent lists Hy3 MMLU-Pro at 65.76; Baidu AI measures 66.9. How does it compare with DeepSeek, Tencent and Xiaomi base models? Feature ERNIE 5.5 Flash Base DeepSeek-V4-Flash-Base Hy3-preview-Base MiMo-V2.5-Base Developer Baidu DeepSeek Tencent Xiaomi Total params 280B 284B 295B (+3.8B MTP) 310B Active params 14B 13B 21B 15B Context 128K train / 1M inference 1M 256K 256K Attention HCA + MLA-DSA hybrid CSA + HCA hybrid GQA SWA + global, 5:1 Experts 512 routed, top-10 + 1 shared Not disclosed on card 192, top-8 256, top-8 Released weights FP8, BF16 FP8 Mixed BF16 FP8 License ERNIE 5.5 Flash Base License v1.0 MIT Tencent Hy Community License MIT MMLU-Pro* 78.4 69.2 66.9 65.7 HumanEval+* 82.3 69.5 78.0 74.4 LongBench-v2* 48.7 44.5 39.8 44.6 HELMET-Rerank* 56.2 60.0 55.7 56.6 *Scores from Baidu’s unified evaluation , self-reported. How do you deploy ERNIE 5.5 Flash Base? Weights are on Hugging Face and ModelScope, in FP8 and BF16 . Baidu documents serving with SGLang and vLLM. The SGLang example uses --tp 4 . The vLLM path needs version 0.32.0 plus the vLLM-ERNIE plugin . Both servers accept up to 1,048,576 tokens. As a base model, it runs through the completions endpoint, not chat. Training ran on FlashMask-4 , a kernel for SM90 and SM100 GPUs. On SM100, Baidu team reports up to 175% faster forward and 74% faster backward than FlashAttention-4 MaskMod. The post Thinking Machines Releases Inkling 2 Small, a 594B MoE With 17B Active appeared first on MarkTechPost . ]]> Thinking Machines Lab has released Inkling 2 Small , the first model of its second Inkling generation. The Inkling 2 Small model is a sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) with 594B total and 17B active parameters. It accepts text and images, and supports variable reasoning effort. On the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index , it scores 31. Its predecessor, Inkling Small , scores 13 on the same index. The model is live on Tinker for fine-tuning and inference. TL;DR Size: 594B total, 17B active MoE; 1M-token context. Runs on: Tinker API only for now. Self-hosting hardware is not disclosed. Weights support MXFP8 and NVFP4. Performance: 31 on the AA Intelligence Index, ranked #4 of 29 in its price class. Best: 86.3% on SWE-Bench Pro v2 (Hard), second only to Kimi K3 in the lab’s table. Worst: 13.1% on Terminal-Bench 4.0, versus 32.8% for GLM-5.3-Flash. What is Inkling 2 Small? Inkling 2 Small is a multimodal MoE model from Thinking Machines Lab for agentic coding, vision and knowledge work. It takes text and image input and returns text. It is important to note that it does not support audio as of now. Weights are closed at launch. The Thinking Machines Lab plans an Apache 2.0 release next week, after external safety testing and red-teaming. This follows its safe path to open weights policy. How is Inkling 2 Small built? It includes a 48-layer decoder-only transformer. Each token routes to 8 of 384 experts. Attention mixes local and global layers. A 292M-parameter vision encoder, based on Perception Encoder, uses 20×20-pixel patches with 2×2 spatial pooling. Image patches are interleaved with text tokens. Pretraining ran in 4 phases: H1: 8.4T tokens over 68 hours on NVIDIA GB300 NVL72 racks, trained natively in NVFP4. H2: 3.8T tokens of newer, higher-quality data at 512K context. H3: about 320B tokens of reasoning and agent trajectories at 1M context. H4: about 34B tokens of the highest-quality agent trajectories. A single joint RL run followed. It took 1,075 steps, 17M+ rollouts and 9 days on 2,048 GPUs. Compute exceeded 4 × 10²³ FLOPs. Coding made up 65.0% of RL tokens. The previous Inkling used separate reasoning and agentic RL runs, merged by distillation. Alignment got explicit attention. Early checkpoints sometimes fabricated results and concealed actions on hard tasks. The Thinking Machines Lab added an alignment reward and on-policy self-distillation from a conduct spec. Its internal misbehavior score fell from 66.8 on Inkling to 14.9. How does Inkling 2 Small perform on benchmarks? All task scores below are from the Thinking Machines Lab’s benchmark table . They run at effort 0.99 (xhigh) and temperature 1.0. Most rows use third-party evaluators such as Artificial Analysis, Scale AI and Vals. Where it scores highest: SWE-Bench Pro v2 (Hard): 86.3%. PerceptionBench: 64.7%, versus 58.5% for Kimi K3. EnterpriseBench-CoreCraft: 71.8%, versus 46.7% for GLM-5.3-Flash. JobBench: 70.5%. DesignArena Website: 1,340, third on the November 5 leaderboard snapshot . Where it trails: Terminal-Bench 4.0: 13.1%, versus 33.8% for DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017. DeepSWE v1.1: 72.1%, versus 77.0% for DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017. GDPVal-AA v2.1: 1,630, versus 1,746 for DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017. On the PMPP-Hard GPU kernel benchmark, it solved 54.25 of 69 tasks on average. In an autoresearch demo, it fine-tuned Qwen3.5-4B for time-series forecasting. It spent $426 of a $500 Tinker budget. The release post cites both 4.5 hours and 4 h 17 min for the run. How does Inkling 2 Small compare with DeepSeek and GLM? Where can developers use it, and what does it cost? Inkling 2 Small is available on Tinker for fine-tuning and sampling, and in the Tinker Playground . Fine-tuning uses the Tinker Cookbook and the tml-renderers package. Checkpoints become downloadable when weights ship. Other platforms are expected in the coming weeks. Artificial Analysis lists pricing at $0.30 per 1M input tokens and $1.00 per 1M output tokens. That is cheaper on output than Inkling Small at $1.20. The company brings together two founders who previously built businesses that help patients get treatment outside a traditional doctor’s office. Jonathan Sabbagh co-founded Journey Clinical , which supports practices offering ketamine-assisted psychotherapy, and Edvard Engesæth co-founded Nurx , which provides birth control and other healthcare services online. Village Global led the financing for New York-based Siggy. Notably, several investors in the round previously backed one or both founders. They include Albert Wenger of Union Square Ventures , Mercury co-founder Immad Akhund , and Cityblock Health co-founder Toyin Ajayi , through Coalition Operators . Other participants include PsyMed Ventures , Mystic Ventures and Gokul Rajaram . Jonathan Sabbagh and Edvard Engesæth, co-founders of Siggy. (Courtesy photo) The founders said they began building Siggy in late 2025. The round, which they plan to use to hire more clinicians and engineers, develop the software and work on regulatory requirements, is the first outside funding for the company. The startup recently began accepting paying patients ahead of its public launch, and the founders said they next plan to test the service with paying patients before expanding further. Between appointments Sabbagh, Siggy’s CEO, told Crunchbase News in an interview that the company is addressing a problem he encountered in mental healthcare. Therapists and the clinicians prescribing their patients’ medication often work separately. Patients may see a therapist weekly but have only a brief appointment every few months with their prescriber. This leaves little time or opportunity to discuss changes in symptoms or medication side effects. To address that problem, Siggy uses AI conversations and daily check-ins to gather information clinicians can review between visits. “AI helps maintain the conversation and organize what patients share, so clinicians have a richer picture of the person that they’re treating,” said Engesæth, the startup’s COO, in an interview. Patients begin by answering questions about their history through a free AI conversation. They then meet a licensed clinician by video, who reviews that information. The clinician then makes a diagnosis and prescribes medication if appropriate. Patients can talk with Siggy’s AI between appointments and can also check in each day to report their sleep, mood, medication and how they feel physically. The company combines those answers with data from connected wearable devices to produce a daily “Siggy Score” out of 100. The score is visible to both the patient and clinician. Patients can opt to connect wearables such as Whoop , Oura or Apple Watch, adding sleep, activity, heart rate and heart rate variability data to the daily check-ins that underpin the Siggy Score. The company aims to use those patterns to flag difficult stretches earlier, including when patients report feeling fine despite worsening sleep or other physical changes. If the score changes, the software flags it for a clinician to review. Patients also receive weekly check-ins during their first eight weeks of treatment, according to the company. Clinicians decide whether to continue treatment or adjust medication, and also handle all medical questions. When appropriate, they can help patients taper off gradually. Siggy does not prescribe controlled substances and is not a crisis service, the founders said. One important note: Patients can continue seeing their existing therapists while using Siggy, Sabbagh said. A planned feature would let patients share information with other providers and involve loved ones in their care. A prior working relationship As with many startup founders, Sabbagh’s interest in mental health treatment grew out of his own experience. After two decades in finance, he experienced burnout and was eventually diagnosed with PTSD related to childhood trauma. He said ketamine-assisted therapy helped him recover, leading him to return to school to study psychology at 38. He subsequently co-founded Journey Clinical. Sabbagh said he has since become its executive chairman, remaining involved while taking on the CEO role at Siggy. Engesæth, a physician by training, was an early investor in Journey and advised Sabbagh as he built the company. Before that, Engesæth co-founded Nurx, which initially helped patients obtain birth control prescriptions and receive medication at home. He said the company grew to more than 2 million patients and an annual revenue run rate exceeding $100 million before merging with Thirty Madison in 2022. The two had considered starting a company together for years. With Siggy, they say they want to make the regular contact and coordination Sabbagh had with his own providers available to more patients. Accepting insurance Siggy accepts commercial insurance in all 50 states and is expanding into government insurance programs. Patients can also pay directly; insured patients’ costs vary by plan. Insurance was a priority because many prospective patients cannot afford treatment out of pocket, Engesæth said. The founders also say Siggy’s service will be permanently free to veterans. Investor POV Amrit Rao , a general partner at Village Global, told Crunchbase News via email that the founders’ experience building healthcare companies was a major reason he invested. The fact that Siggy accepts insurance was important too. “Pairing that vision with an insurance-based model makes the ambition about access as much as technology,” he said. Mercury co-founder and CEO Immad Akhund, who invested personally, is a repeat backer of both founders. newContent: Crunchbase News https://news.crunchbase.com/ Data-driven reporting on private markets, startups, founders, and investors Thu, 05 Nov 2026 19:02:26 +0000 en-US hourly 1 https://wordpress.org/?v=6.8.12 https://news.crunchbase.com/wp-content/uploads/cb_news_favicon-150x150.png Crunchbase News https://news.crunchbase.com/ 32 32 How To Challenge A Monopoly In The AI Age https://news.crunchbase.com/ai/challenging-monopolies-semiconductors-anand-tensordyn/ Fri, 06 Nov 2026 12:00:08 +0000 https://news.crunchbase.com/?p=94339 By R K Anand If you were in Silicon Valley in the late 1990s, today’s AI boom might feel familiar. In 1998 and 1999, internet traffic was roughly doubling every six to nine months. That was extraordinary growth in demand, and still, that pales in comparison to what we’re seeing unfold now. Today, the four largest U.S. cloud companies are looking at more than $700 billion in capital spending this year, and the cumulative AI infrastructure spending is projected to reach $3 trillion to $4 trillion by 2030. R K Anand of Tensordyne. Nvidia arguably fired the starting gun in AI chips when Jensen Huang hand-delivered its DGX-1 to OpenAI in 2016. Today, it is a household name deeply embedded in the AI ecosystem, working with near-exclusive supply and investment deals. With such a huge market under a seeming monopoly, where can competition — and the innovation that follows it — come from? Part of the answer is that scale costs you speed, though when going up against an execution machine like Nvidia this is simply the baseline you have to solve for. The pace of change in AI outruns anything we saw in previous tech cycles: Model generations turn over in weeks, not years. The hardware beneath it has to keep shifting to serve them, and designing from first principles has real merit. Lessons from Davids that came before Hardware suppliers of the dot-com era followed the same peaks and troughs. Cisco , founded in 1984, dominated internet routing for most of the decade, and in March 2000 it was the highest market capitalization company in the world. Then Juniper Networks , a startup where I was a founding engineer, shipped its first core router in 1998. Juniper went from a fairly anonymous upstart to 17% of the core router market at the end of 1999, then again to 38% in early 2001. Challengers now can lean on history for some guidance. First, don’t build a cheaper version of the incumbent’s product. Build a far better one. At Juniper, our bet was that the then-adolescent version of the internet was going to demand an exponentially higher throughput than before. Introducing an entirely new architectural approach to how routers are built, along with an innovative design philosophy focused on performance and reliability, we didn’t set out to sell a better router, so much as redefine what a core router had to be. The boom in AI inference is today’s version of that strain on throughput. The initial hyperfixation on training AI models is fading, and the industry is collectively moving on to using them — known as inference. Inference is where AI’s promised productivity gains actually materialize, putting trained models to work across every task. As the enterprise applications for AI grow and become more complex, so too does demand for inference compute. Google recently reported that it now processes more than 3.2 quadrillion tokens a month, up from 480 trillion a year earlier, as AI moves from chat to agents that plan and act on our behalf. Serving tokens at scale is a different beast from when it was just for model training, with different constraints on memory, power and cost. The core principle we use applies to all sectors: Challengers have a better chance at optimizing for the market that will come, not the market that is already well-serviced by the incumbent. Be known by your track record Challengers start without the incumbent’s biggest asset: a reputation. Buying from the market leader is the safe choice, so a startup has to replace that trust with evidence. Every technological edge you can demonstrate and validate makes the next conversation easier, and over time that compounds into the credibility that an incumbent may take for granted. To aid this, make migration as easy as possible. No one is wedded to a product out of loyalty. Inertia is one of the biggest strengths of an incumbent: the ease of continuing to do what has been done. Unless there are clear economic and operational benefits, scale and performance advantages, more often than not, integrating new systems will not be worth the work involved in switching suppliers. Take any technical friction out of the equation, and you have a fighting chance with your improved product. Uncertainty is your friend The internet transformed the world in ways that we couldn’t have predicted, and I have little doubt that the relentless pace and momentum of AI is resulting in changes that are quickly making our lives and work unrecognizable from the recent past. This is only going to accelerate. Monopolies in frontier technology look insurmountable right up until the work changes. What AI does is rapidly morphing and evolving. There is comfort in that for founders, and in something else too: A small team can now achieve so much. Challenging Cisco in the late 90s and early 2000s meant building a nimble and dynamic organization, albeit much smaller — one that is far more capable, reactive and product-focused. Juniper numbered a few hundred people by the time it had significant market traction, compared to the thousands of employees at Cisco. Our own company is now around 120 people, attempting what once took an army. That is what should keep the incumbents watching. R K Anand is co-founder and chief product officer of Tensordyne , an AI inference company. He was a founding engineer and executive vice president of the data center business unit at Juniper Networks and began his career designing microprocessors at Sun Microsystems .
